extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants (small businesses, independent inventors), patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on when and how to file a Request for Continued Examination (RCE) in U.S. patent prosecution: eligibility triggers, required contents, timing, strategic benefits, exceptions, IDS interplay, likely outcomes, and alternatives to filing an RCE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility / trigger for filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE may be filed only after issuance of a Final Office Action—defined as a final rejection of a patent application, a Notice of Allowance, or an action that otherwise ends prosecution in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that an RCE is a request made after a 'final determination' and is the mechanism to continue examination once prosecution has been concluded by a Final Office Action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE must be submitted within four months of the Final Office Action (extensions can be obtained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File promptly after finality; extensions are possible but timeliness is a statutory/practical constraint to preserve the ability to reopen prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a written RCE request
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly filed RCE must include: the proper request form; payment of the proper fees; an information disclosure statement (IDS); and new justifications or supporting information for the patentability of the written description, claims, or drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All listed elements are required for the PTO to continue processing the application; omission may prevent the RCE from taking effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of filing an RCE on prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon correct filing and fee payment, the Final Office Action’s finality is withdrawn, prosecution is reopened, and the claims are assessed as though being made for the first time in a newly filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes the RCE 'resets the clock'—the examiner gets an additional block of examiner time, and subsequent rejections will not be the previous final one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary benefits of filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE is often faster and less expensive than an appeal; it provides more examiner time, keeps the application pending (strategic benefit), and allows substantive amendments/arguments that are limited in after-final responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained benefits include cost/time advantages vs PTAB appeal, resetting examiner time allocation, strategic desire to keep application pending, and ability to present arguments/claim amendments that would otherwise require new prior art searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: When filing an RCE is recommended (substantive reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE may be advisable if the examiner appears to have made a legal mistake or if a thorough review of specific prior art could change the Final Office Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when there is reason to believe further examination/review will alter the outcome — e.g., legal errors by the examiner or overlooked prior art that justifies reopening prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions / application types not eligible for RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: RCEs are not available for: provisional applications; utility/plant applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) before June 8, 1995; international applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 363 before June 8, 1995 or international applications not complying with 35 U.S.C. 371; design patent applications; international design applications; and patents under re-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides a concrete list of ineligible application categories — check application type and filing dates to confirm RCE eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations when an RCE is unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE is unnecessary if the examiner suggested a particular claim would be allowed (you can submit an after-final response incorporating the suggested language), or if only minor claim restrictions are contemplated (consider AFCP). If the examiner will not enter an after-final response, they will issue an Advisory Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before automatically filing an RCE, consider after-final responses, the After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP), and whether the intended changes truly require reopening prosecution and additional examiner search time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic guidance on when to file an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: File an RCE when you want to make additional claim revisions and/or arguments after a Final Office Action, particularly if your changes will require the examiner to perform more extensive prior-art searching. An examiner interview before filing can help determine necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recommends an examiner interview as a diagnostic step to see whether an RCE is required and to understand the examiner’s view on whether the claims merit further time.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS timing rule related to RCE filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an IDS can be filed without first filing an RCE depends on the date the applicant first became aware of the prior art: if the earliest date of awareness is less than three months before the IDS is filed, the applicant can avoid an RCE and pay a small fee; if awareness occurred more than three months before the IDS due date, the applicant must file an RCE before submitting the IDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date-of-awareness calculations matter for IDS practice — if too much time elapsed, an RCE is required before an IDS can be accepted without additional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of RCEs and practical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory limit on the number of RCEs an applicant may file, but after one or more RCEs and diminishing prospects with a particular examiner, an appeal may be more cost-effective than filing additional RCEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although unlimited in theory, multiple RCEs can be a poor strategic choice; assess cost-benefit and the efficacy of continuing before the same examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likely outcomes after filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: After an RCE is filed, the examiner may approve the application (possibly in combination with an Office Action response) or issue a further, usually non-final Office Action (giving the applicant another chance to respond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect either allowance or further prosecution; a non-final action restarts back-and-forth and may lead to more prosecution choices (continue or abandon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives include filing a continuation application, appealing to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), submitting an after-final response possibly with AFCP participation, or using AFCP 2.0 when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoffs: continuation delays examination (you wait in the queue), appeals are slower but may obtain expanded protection, AFCP/after-final may avoid RCE only when very limited changes are needed. The page recommends considering these alternatives based on cost, timing, and likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: AFCP 2.0 eligibility and process notes
rubrics_metrics.description: AFCP 2.0 can be requested following receipt of a final office action but is appropriate only if the examiner believes the claims are almost certain to be accepted; the applicant must request AFCP 2.0 during an examiner interview. If the examiner does not agree, an RCE must be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFCP 2.0 is a narrow pilot route to avoid an RCE when allowance is highly likely — it requires examiner concurrence obtained in an interview.
